cards.prompt: Cosmic Shoes' admin is building a new agent in Agent Builder and needs to define what the agent is allowed to discuss and do within a specific area of the business, such as order status inquiries. Which agent building block should the admin configure first for this purpose?
options: A permission set
A page layout
A Topic
A validation rule
answer: A Topic
cards.why: This tests the basic anatomy of an Agentforce agent. A Topic is a named job area (for example, Order Status) made of a description, a scope (what the agent may and may not do there), instructions, and the actions the agent may run while in that topic. When a customer asks something, the agent first classifies the request into a topic, then picks from that topic's actions. You build topics in Agentforce Builder (newer builder screens may call them subagents). Rule of thumb: 'what area can the agent handle and what can it do there' = Topic.

translate.situation: Tell the agent what one area of the business covers, e.g., order status.
translate.see: A named topic with instructions and the actions it may use.
translate.notOther: Permission sets control who can use the agent, not what it talks about.

cards.traps: Security and UI features (permission sets, layouts) dressed up as agent-building blocks.
cards.strip: Agentforce · define what agent covers in one business area · scope + instructions + actions → Topic

wrong.A permission set: Permission sets control what users (or the agent's running user) can access. They don't define what subject area the agent talks about.
wrong.A page layout: Page layouts arrange fields and related lists on a record page. They have nothing to do with an agent's conversation scope.
wrong.A validation rule: Validation rules block bad data from being saved on a record. They don't define an agent's job area or actions.

cards.prompt: An administrator wants to ensure that when Agentforce generates email drafts, sensitive customer credit card numbers stored in the case description are never visible to an external Large Language Model (LLM) provider. Which Einstein Trust Layer capability directly prevents this sensitive data from being shared with the LLM?
options: Prompt Defense
PII/Data Masking
Zero Data Retention
Toxic Language Detection
answer: PII/Data Masking
cards.why: The Einstein Trust Layer is the set of safeguards between Salesforce data and the outside LLM (large language model, the AI that writes text). Data masking detects sensitive values like credit card numbers, emails, or names in the prompt and swaps them for placeholder tokens before the prompt leaves Salesforce; the real values are put back when the response returns. So the external provider never sees the card number at all. You manage masking settings in Setup under Einstein Trust Layer. Rule of thumb: 'the LLM must never see it' = masking; 'the LLM must not keep it' = zero data retention.
cards.traps: Zero Data Retention sounds protective, but it governs storage after the fact, not visibility.
cards.strip: Trust Layer · keep card numbers away from external LLM · never visible → Data Masking

wrong.Prompt Defense: Prompt defense adds guardrail instructions to resist prompt-injection and jailbreak attempts. It doesn't hide data values inside the prompt.
wrong.Zero Data Retention: Zero data retention means the provider doesn't store or train on what it receives, but the provider still sees the data during processing. The question asks to keep it from being seen at all.
wrong.Toxic Language Detection: Toxicity detection scores prompts and responses for harmful or offensive language. It doesn't remove sensitive data.

cards.prompt: Global Containers has created a Performance Review App and would like to ensure that only the manager of a staff member and managers further up the chain in the same department have visibility to the review of a staff member. The role hierarchy does not follow the organization structure. How can this be configured?
options: Ensure that the 'Grant Access Using Hierarchies' Checkbox is deselected
Ensure that the role hierarchy reflects the reporting hierarchy
Ensure that the 'Grant Access Using Hierarchies' Checkbox is selected
Ensure that the 'Manager Groups' setting is selected on the Sharing Settings page
Create a sharing rule to share Performance Reviews with the user's manager group
answer: Ensure that the 'Grant Access Using Hierarchies' Checkbox is deselected
Ensure that the 'Manager Groups' setting is selected on the Sharing Settings page
Create a sharing rule to share Performance Reviews with the user's manager group
cards.why: This tests sharing when the role hierarchy doesn't match the reporting (manager) chain. First, on a custom object you can uncheck 'Grant Access Using Hierarchies' in Sharing Settings so the role hierarchy stops opening records upward; otherwise people in higher roles who aren't in the manager chain would see reviews. Second, enable Manager Groups in Sharing Settings; this creates a group for each user containing their manager and that manager's managers (based on the Manager field on the user record). Third, create a sharing rule (or manual share) that shares Performance Review records with the owner's Manager Group. Rule of thumb: 'manager chain, not role chain' = Manager Groups plus sharing, with hierarchy access turned off.

translate.situation: Only someone's real managers (the 'Manager' field chain) should see their review, not whoever ranks higher in roles.
translate.feature: Manager Groups + a sharing rule, with 'Grant Access Using Hierarchies' turned off.
translate.see: Reviews are visible to the person's manager and that manager's manager, nobody else.
translate.notOther: Leaving hierarchy access on lets anyone above in the role tree see it; the role tree doesn't match real managers here.

cards.traps: 'Make the role hierarchy match' sounds tidy but is a sledgehammer; Manager Groups exist for this exact case.
cards.strip: Sharing · only manager chain sees review · role hierarchy ≠ org chart → uncheck hierarchy access + Manager Groups + sharing rule

wrong.Ensure that the role hierarchy reflects: Reorganizing the whole role hierarchy to fix one app would break sharing for every other object, and the question states the hierarchy doesn't follow the org chart for a reason.
wrong.Ensure that the 'Grant Access Using Hier: Leaving it selected lets everyone above the owner in the role hierarchy see the reviews, which is exactly the leak to avoid.

cards.prompt: Which of the following can be added to a custom page layout?
options: List views
Custom fields
Validation rules
Record types
answer: Custom fields
cards.why: A page layout controls what appears on a record page: fields, related lists, buttons, quick actions, sections, and some components. Custom fields (and standard fields) are dragged onto the layout from the palette in Object Manager > [Object] > Page Layouts. The other options are separate configuration items, not things you place on a layout. Rule of thumb: layouts hold fields, related lists, buttons, and actions.
cards.traps: Things that relate to layouts (record types, list views) vs. things that sit on a layout.
cards.strip: Page layout · what can be added · items placed on the record page → Custom fields

wrong.List views: List views are filtered lists of records shown on an object's tab or list page, not on a single record's layout.
wrong.Validation rules: Validation rules run when a record is saved, no matter which layout is used. They're defined on the object, not placed on a layout.
wrong.Record types: Record types are assigned to page layouts (each record type can use a different layout), but you can't add a record type onto a layout.

cards.prompt: An administrator is considering deleting a custom text field on the Account object that is thought to be no longer needed. What is true regarding a deleted field?
options: It can never be recovered
It can be recovered at any time
It can be recovered within 30 days of deletion
It can be recovered within 15 days of deletion
answer: It can be recovered within 15 days of deletion
cards.why: When you delete a custom field, Salesforce soft-deletes it: it moves to the object's Deleted Fields list (Object Manager > [Object] > Fields & Relationships > Deleted Fields) for 15 days. During those 15 days you can undelete it and its data comes back, though some settings (like being on layouts or in reports) may need re-adding. After 15 days it is permanently erased. Rule of thumb: deleted fields = 15 days; deleted records in the Recycle Bin = also 15 days.
cards.strip: Deleted custom field · how long recoverable · soft delete window → 15 days

wrong.It can never be recovered: Recovery is possible for 15 days after deletion from the Deleted Fields list.
wrong.It can be recovered at any time: The recovery window is limited; after 15 days the field and its data are permanently deleted.
wrong.It can be recovered within 30 days of de: 30 days is a common distractor; the actual window for deleted custom fields is 15 days.

cards.prompt: An administrator is told to look through the login forensics to spot any suspicious attempts to gain access to the org. Which of the following can login forensics provide?
options: The number of logins per profile.
The average number of logins per user per a specified time period
Who logged in more than the average number of times
Who logged in during non-business hours
The number of logins per role and profile
answer: The average number of logins per user per a specified time period
Who logged in more than the average number of times
Who logged in during non-business hours
cards.why: Login Forensics is part of Event Monitoring (a paid security add-on, via Salesforce Shield) and looks for unusual login behavior per user. It can show the average number of logins per user over a time period, flag users who log in more than that average, and flag users who log in during non-business hours or from suspicious IP ranges. It works on individual user login patterns from login history and login events. Rule of thumb: Login Forensics answers 'which user is behaving oddly,' not 'how many logins per profile or role.'

translate.situation: Spot unusual login behavior.
translate.see: Average logins per user, who's above average, who logged in after hours or from suspicious IPs.
translate.notOther: It doesn't break logins down by role or profile.

cards.traps: Aggregate counts by profile/role sound plausible but Forensics is per-user anomaly detection.
cards.strip: Login Forensics · what it shows · suspicious user patterns → per-user average, above-average users, off-hours logins

Login Forensics focuses on per-user behavior, not totals grouped by profile. You could build a login history report for that, but it isn't a Login Forensics metric.
wrong.The number of logins per role and profil: Grouping by role and profile isn't what Login Forensics provides; it identifies suspicious individual users.

cards.prompt: The Support Director of Cosmic Service Solutions has asked the Salesforce Administrator to add a filter to the 'Contact' field on case records. The field should only allow contacts to be selected if they are associated with the account in the 'Account Name' field. What is the best way to meet this requirement?
options: Create a validation rule that checks whether the contact is related to the account on the case
It is not possible to restrict contacts in this way
Create a picklist for an account and one for contact and make them dependent
Create a dependent lookup on the contact field that references the account field
answer: Create a dependent lookup on the contact field that references the account field
cards.why: This is a lookup filter, sometimes called a dependent lookup. You edit the Contact lookup field on Case (Object Manager > Case > Fields & Relationships > Contact Name > Lookup Filter) and add criteria like 'Contact: Account ID equals Case: Account ID'. The lookup search then only offers contacts that belong to the case's account, and you can make it required (blocks saving) or optional (just a suggestion). Rule of thumb: 'only show records in a lookup that match another field on this record' = lookup filter.

translate.situation: When picking a contact on a case, only show that account's contacts.
translate.see: The Contact search only offers people from the chosen account.
translate.notOther: A validation rule only errors after you pick wrong; a picklist can't replace a lookup.

cards.traps: Validation rule vs. lookup filter: one rejects after the fact, the other limits the choices up front.
cards.strip: Lookup field · only contacts of the case's account · restrict choices → Lookup filter (dependent lookup)

wrong.Create a validation rule that checks whe: A validation rule only throws an error after the user picks the wrong contact and saves. It doesn't filter the choices the user sees, so it's not the best fit.
wrong.It is not possible to restrict contacts: It is possible; lookup filters can compare the target record to fields on the source record.
wrong.Create a picklist for an account and one: Dependent picklists work with fixed lists of values, not live records. You'd have to hard-code every account and contact, which is unmaintainable.

cards.prompt: The Salesforce org of Cosmic Sporting Goods has a Security Health Check score of 75%. Based on the Salesforce Baseline Standard, which grade does this score correspond to in Salesforce?
options: Satisfactory
Good
Acceptable
Fair
answer: Good
cards.why: Health Check (Setup > Health Check) compares your org's security settings against the Salesforce Baseline Standard and gives a score from 0 to 100%. The score bands are: 90% and above = Excellent, 80–89% = Very Good, 70–79% = Good, 55–69% = Poor, 54% and below = Very Poor. So 75% is Good. Rule of thumb: memorize 90/80/70/55 as the cut lines.

translate.situation: Rate how secure the org's settings are.
translate.see: A 75% shows as 'Good'.
translate.notOther: 'Satisfactory', 'Acceptable', 'Fair' aren't grades Salesforce uses.

cards.traps: Made-up grade names that sound right; only Excellent, Very Good, Good, Poor, Very Poor exist.
cards.strip: Health Check · 75% score · baseline bands → Good

wrong.Satisfactory: Satisfactory isn't one of the Health Check grade labels.
wrong.Acceptable: Acceptable isn't a Health Check grade label.
wrong.Fair: Fair isn't a Health Check grade label; the band below Good is Poor.

cards.prompt: The Marketing department would like to have a visual representation for tracking the lifecycle stages of campaign records with guidance similar to what Sales utilizes for Opportunities in Lightning Experience. How can the Salesforce Administrator help accomplish this?
options: Create a new picklist and a new path, then modify the Campaign page in Lightning Experience
Create a new picklist and modify the Campaign page in Lightning Experience
Create a new picklist, record type, and modify the Campaign page in Lightning Experience
It cannot be accomplished. Only opportunities can have this visual representation
answer: Create a new picklist and a new path, then modify the Campaign page in Lightning Experience
cards.why: Path is the chevron bar across the top of a record that shows stages, with optional key fields and guidance text for each stage. Path works on many objects, including Campaigns, not just Opportunities. You make sure there's a picklist that holds the lifecycle stages (Campaign's Status or a new custom picklist), create the path in Setup > Path Settings choosing that picklist, add key fields and guidance, then add the Path component to the Campaign Lightning record page in Lightning App Builder. Rule of thumb: 'visual stages with guidance' = Path, which needs a picklist.
cards.traps: Answers that list ingredients but skip the actual Path setup step.
cards.strip: Campaign · visual stages with guidance like Opportunities · Lightning → picklist + Path + add to page

wrong.Create a new picklist and modify the Cam: A picklist alone gives no visual stage bar or guidance; you still need to create the Path itself.
wrong.Create a new picklist, record type, and: Record types are optional for Path (a path can be per record type), but without creating a Path there's still no visual stage tracker.
wrong.It cannot be accomplished. Only opportun: Path supports Campaigns, Leads, Accounts, Contacts, Cases, Orders, Quotes, custom objects, and more.

cards.prompt: For any customer-centric organization, the opportunity or deal record data are sensitive. A sales manager has requested the Salesforce Administrator to monitor some of the important fields that are getting changed by multiple teams from time to time during the sales lifecycle. Which security option can the Salesforce Administrator choose to achieve this?
options: Provide the 'View All' permission to the sales manager to allow seeing all changes.
Provide the 'View All Data' permission to the sales manager to allow seeing all changes
Enable field history tracking for the opportunity object and create a report
Enable organization-wide default sharing settings for the opportunity object to set it to the sales manager level
answer: Enable field history tracking for the opportunity object and create a report
cards.why: Field history tracking records old value, new value, who changed it, and when, for up to 20 chosen fields per object. You turn it on in Object Manager > Opportunity > Fields & Relationships > Set History Tracking, pick the fields, then report on it with the 'Opportunity Field History' report type (or show the history related list). That lets the manager monitor changes across teams. Rule of thumb: 'see who changed a field and when' = field history tracking.
cards.traps: Access permissions posing as auditing features.
cards.strip: Opportunity · monitor field changes · who/when/old/new → Field history tracking + report

wrong.Provide the 'View All' permission to the: View All lets someone see every record of an object, but seeing records doesn't show their change history.
wrong.Provide the 'View All Data' permission t: View All Data is an admin-level permission to see every record in the org. It's far too broad and still doesn't log field changes.
wrong.Enable organization-wide default sharing: Org-wide defaults set baseline record access, and there's no 'sales manager level' setting. Sharing doesn't track changes.

cards.prompt: A Salesforce Administrator has defined a new custom object and has identified that it needs to have a many-to-many relationship with 5 different standard objects. What considerations should the Salesforce Administrator keep in mind when designing the solution?
options: It depends on the remaining custom object quota left in the org
Not feasible, since only up to three master-detail relationships are possible on a custom object
Not feasible, since only two many-to-many relationships are allowed per object
Not feasible, since only up to two master-detail relationships are possible on a custom object
answer: It depends on the remaining custom object quota left in the org
cards.why: A many-to-many relationship in Salesforce is built with a junction object: a custom object with two master-detail fields, one to each side. An object can have only two master-detail relationships, so one junction object can link just two objects. To relate the new custom object to 5 standard objects many-to-many, you'd need 5 separate junction objects, each one a custom object. So the real constraint is whether the org's edition still has room for that many more custom objects. Rule of thumb: each many-to-many = one new junction object.

translate.situation: Connect one custom object many-to-many with five others.
translate.see: Five new 'link' objects, each with two master-detail fields.
translate.notOther: The 2-master-detail limit sits on each junction, not on the main object, so it's allowed.

cards.traps: The true '2 master-details' fact used to reach the wrong conclusion.
cards.strip: Many-to-many × 5 · feasibility · each needs a junction object → depends on remaining custom object quota

wrong.Not feasible, since only up to three mas: The limit is two master-detail relationships per object, not three, and the design uses separate junction objects anyway.
wrong.Not feasible, since only two many-to-man: There's no rule limiting an object to two many-to-many relationships; you can have as many as you have junction objects.
wrong.Not feasible, since only up to two maste: The two-master-detail limit is real but applies to each junction object, and each junction only needs two. With five junction objects, the design is feasible.

cards.prompt: A Salesforce Administrator often deals with record-level security. Which of the following are correct regarding record-level security?
options: Roles are used to open up the record access among the user groups (i.e. horizontally).
Organization-wide sharing defaults are always used for opening record access to the user
Sharing rules can never be stricter than the organization-wide sharing defaults
Roles are used to create a sharing hierarchy among the users.
answer: Sharing rules can never be stricter than the organization-wide sharing defaults
Roles are used to create a sharing hierarchy among the users.
cards.why: Record-level security works in layers. Org-wide defaults (OWD) set the most restrictive baseline access; everything else can only open access further. The role hierarchy opens access vertically: users higher up can see records owned by people below them. Sharing rules open access sideways to groups, roles, or territories, and can never take access away below the OWD. Rule of thumb: OWD locks down, then roles, sharing rules, and manual sharing open up.

translate.situation: Understand which tool restricts and which opens record access.
translate.feature: OWD (floor), roles (up the hierarchy), sharing rules (sideways).
translate.see: Managers see their team's records; sharing rules add access, never remove it.
translate.notOther: Roles open access UP, not sideways; OWD restricts, it doesn't open.

cards.traps: Horizontal vs. vertical: roles = up/down, sharing rules = across.
cards.strip: Record-level security · true statements · OWD restricts, others open → sharing rules can't restrict; roles create hierarchy

wrong.Roles are used to open up the record acc: Roles open access vertically (up the hierarchy). Horizontal access between peers is what sharing rules are for.
wrong.Organization-wide sharing defaults are a: OWDs set the most restrictive baseline; they're used to lock down access, and other tools open it up.

cards.prompt: What happens when a lead is converted?
options: The owner of the records created can be selected right before conversion
The lead is visible in the Leads tab with a status of 'Converted' by default
Opportunities are always created for converted leads
A name is generated automatically for the opportunity during the lead conversion process
answer: The owner of the records created can be selected right before conversion
A name is generated automatically for the opportunity during the lead conversion process
cards.why: Lead conversion turns a lead into an Account, a Contact, and optionally an Opportunity. On the Convert screen you can choose the record owner for the new records before you click Convert. Salesforce also pre-fills an opportunity name automatically (based on the company name), which you can edit. Rule of thumb: on conversion you pick the owner, the opportunity is optional, and the converted lead disappears from normal lead views.

translate.situation: Turn a qualified lead into an account, contact, and maybe a deal.
translate.see: A convert screen where you pick the record owner and see a pre-filled opportunity name.
translate.notOther: Converted leads disappear from the Leads tab by default; opportunity creation is optional.

cards.traps: 'Always' about the opportunity; it's optional.
cards.strip: Lead conversion · what happens · Convert screen → owner chosen; opportunity name auto-generated

wrong.The lead is visible in the Leads tab wit: Converted leads are hidden from lead list views and search; only users with the 'View and Edit Converted Leads' permission can see them.
wrong.Opportunities are always created for con: Creating an opportunity is optional; you can check 'Don't create an opportunity upon conversion.'

cards.prompt: The Salesforce Administrator of Cosmic Solutions is worried about an upcoming release update that is critical and the changes it can cause to the customizations of the org. What are true about the release updates from Salesforce's seasonal releases?
options: Release updates are applied only after an administrator reviews them in the Sandbox org.
Release updates are applied only after an administrator reviews them in the Production org.
Release updates have steps for an administrator to follow to understand their impact on the org and then choose to apply the update before the enforcement date.
Release updates are automatically applied to the Production org on the enforcement date announced.
answer: Release updates have steps for an administrator to follow to understand their impact on the org and then choose to apply the update before the enforcement date.
Release updates are automatically applied to the Production org on the enforcement date announced.
cards.why: Release updates (Setup > Release Updates) are changes Salesforce schedules that could affect existing customizations. Each one lists steps to help you understand the impact, and you can test and turn it on early, ideally in a sandbox first. If you don't act, Salesforce enforces it automatically on the announced enforcement date. Rule of thumb: release updates are opt-in early, mandatory later.

translate.situation: Salesforce is changing behavior in an upcoming release.
translate.see: A page listing each update, its test steps, and its enforcement date.
translate.notOther: They don't wait for your review; they apply automatically on the date.

cards.traps: 'Only after an admin reviews' — Salesforce doesn't wait for you.
cards.strip: Release updates · how they apply · enforcement date → steps to test/apply early; auto-applied on enforcement date

wrong.Release updates are applied only after a: Testing in a sandbox is recommended but not required; the update is enforced on its date whether or not anyone reviewed it.
Admin review isn't a prerequisite; Salesforce applies the update automatically on the enforcement date.

cards.prompt: What is a key capability of Quotes and Orders in the sales process in Salesforce?
options: Tracking customer interactions and communications
Generating invoices and processing payments
Creating and managing leads
Managing price quotes and sales agreements
answer: Managing price quotes and sales agreements
cards.why: Quotes and Orders are standard objects in the later part of the sales cycle. A Quote, tied to an Opportunity, lists products, prices, and discounts to send to the customer; it can be generated as a PDF. An Order records what the customer agreed to buy, usually tied to an Account and a Contract. Together they manage pricing proposals and confirmed sales agreements. Rule of thumb: Quote = price proposal, Order = confirmed purchase.

translate.situation: Send a customer a price offer, then record what they agreed to buy.
translate.see: A quote PDF with products and prices; an order confirming the deal.
translate.notOther: Invoicing and payments need other products or integrations.

cards.traps: Invoicing sounds like the next step after an order, but it isn't core Quotes/Orders.
cards.strip: Quotes & Orders · key capability · late sales cycle → manage price quotes and sales agreements

wrong.Tracking customer interactions and commu: That's Activities (tasks, events, emails) on the activity timeline.
wrong.Generating invoices and processing payme: Standard Sales Cloud doesn't invoice or take payments; that's billing products like Revenue Cloud or Salesforce Billing.
wrong.Creating and managing leads: Leads are managed with the Lead object, before any quote exists.

cards.prompt: A Salesforce Administrator would like to absolutely deny login access to the company's Salesforce org if users are logging in outside the specified login hours and IP range. What are the different options that can be used?
options: Profile-based login hour restrictions
Organization-based login hour restrictions
Profile based IP restrictions
Organization-wide IP restrictions
answer: Profile-based login hour restrictions
Profile based IP restrictions
cards.why: To fully block logins outside allowed times or networks, use profile settings. Login Hours on a profile block login outside the set hours (and log out active users when the time ends). Login IP Ranges on a profile block login from any IP outside the list. Both are set on the profile (Setup > Profiles > [Profile] > Login Hours / Login IP Ranges). Rule of thumb: profile = hard block; org-wide Network Access trusted IPs = skip the verification code, not a block.

translate.situation: Hard-block logins outside set hours or locations.
translate.feature: Profile Login Hours + Profile Login IP Ranges.
translate.see: Login denied outright.
translate.notOther: Org-wide trusted IPs just ask for a verification code; org-wide login hours don't exist.

cards.traps: Org-wide trusted IPs look like a block but are only a verification bypass.
cards.strip: Login access · absolutely deny outside hours/IP · hard block → profile login hours + profile IP ranges

wrong.Organization-based login hour restrictio: There's no org-wide login hours setting; login hours exist only on profiles.
wrong.Organization-wide IP restrictions: Org-wide trusted IP ranges (Setup > Network Access) only decide whether users get a verification challenge. Users outside the range can still log in after verifying, so it doesn't deny access.

cards.prompt: For a new product launch, campaigns have been set up to track responses from the website, print advertisement, and direct marketing activities. How can the cumulative figures from various campaign strategies be made visible and tracked within the primary product launch campaign?
options: Create a report that totals the opportunities related to each campaign
Create a campaign hierarchy linking the campaigns and view the campaign statistics on the parent campaign
Create a master-detail relationship between the campaigns and use roll-up summary fields to display the totals
Create a trigger that calculates the number and value of opportunities related to the campaigns and display on each campaign
answer: Create a campaign hierarchy linking the campaigns and view the campaign statistics on the parent campaign
cards.why: A campaign hierarchy links child campaigns (website, print, direct mail) to a parent campaign using the Parent Campaign lookup. The parent campaign then automatically shows hierarchy totals, like total leads, contacts, responses, opportunities, and won opportunity value across all its children. You view these in the Campaign Hierarchy section or fields like 'Total Responses in Hierarchy'. Rule of thumb: 'roll up results from several campaigns into one' = campaign hierarchy.

translate.situation: See combined results of several campaigns under one umbrella campaign.
translate.see: The parent campaign shows 'Total ... in Hierarchy' fields.
translate.notOther: No custom build needed; the totals are standard fields.

cards.traps: Code or roll-up builds for something Salesforce does natively.
cards.strip: Campaigns · totals from several campaigns on main campaign · built-in → Campaign hierarchy

wrong.Create a report that totals the opportun: A report could show numbers but wouldn't put the totals on the parent campaign record, and it only covers opportunities, not responses.
wrong.Create a master-detail relationship betw: You can't create a master-detail relationship between campaigns (an object can't be master-detail to itself), and it isn't needed.
wrong.Create a trigger that calculates the num: Writing Apex code is unnecessary when campaign hierarchies give the totals with no code.

cards.prompt: What are the different ways that data can be backed up?
options: Run a backup manually using Data Export
Schedule a daily data backup using Data Export
Send an email request to Salesforce to export a copy of all data
Export data using Data Loader
answer: Run a backup manually using Data Export
Export data using Data Loader
cards.why: Data Export (Setup > Data Export) creates a ZIP of CSV files with your org's data. You can run it manually ('Export Now') or schedule it, but only weekly (Enterprise and above) or monthly, not daily. Data Loader can also export (or 'Export All' including deleted records) any object to CSV, so it works as a backup method too. Rule of thumb: Data Export = weekly/monthly; Data Loader = on demand, can be scheduled via its command line.
cards.traps: 'Daily' with Data Export; the scheduler only offers weekly or monthly.
cards.strip: Backups · ways to back up · Data Export limits → manual Data Export + Data Loader export

wrong.Schedule a daily data backup using Data: Data Export can only be scheduled weekly or monthly, not daily.
wrong.Send an email request to Salesforce to e: Salesforce doesn't provide backups by email request. Its Data Recovery Service is a paid last resort, not a backup method.

cards.prompt: A Salesforce Administrator wishes to delegate the responsibility of resetting passwords and creating new users to her assistant. The Salesforce Administrator does not wish to give her assistant full administrative rights. What is the most appropriate solution in this case?
options: Create a custom profile and give only limited access to create users and reset passwords
Assign the user to a delegated group that has selected user administration permissions
Open a case with Salesforce for this type of profile creation
Create a custom profile and give administrator permission to it
answer: Assign the user to a delegated group that has selected user administration permissions
cards.why: Delegated administration lets an admin hand off specific admin tasks without giving full admin rights. In Setup > Delegated Administration you create a delegated group, add the assistant as a delegated administrator, and specify which roles they can manage users for (create, edit, reset passwords, unlock) and which profiles/permission sets they can assign. The assistant can only manage users in those roles. Rule of thumb: 'let someone manage users without being an admin' = delegated administration.
cards.traps: Custom profile with 'limited' user management sounds right but Manage Users isn't limited.
cards.strip: User admin · reset passwords + create users · no full admin rights → Delegated administration

wrong.Create a custom profile and give only li: The profile permission 'Manage Users' isn't fine-grained; it lets someone manage all users and assign any profile, which is close to full admin power.
wrong.Open a case with Salesforce for this typ: Admins can set this up themselves; Salesforce Support doesn't create profiles for you.
wrong.Create a custom profile and give adminis: That gives full admin rights, which the admin explicitly wants to avoid.

cards.prompt: Which of the following statements are true about accessing telephony features in Salesforce using Sales Dialer?
options: It is only available in Lightning Experience
It supports incoming and outgoing calls
It requires a feature license in Lightning Experience and Salesforce Classic
Users can call by clicking on phone number fields
It supports recording calls using an additional plugin
answer: It is only available in Lightning Experience
It supports incoming and outgoing calls
Users can call by clicking on phone number fields

cards.prompt: Adam wants to delete an account and the 15 contacts associated with the account. Which method should he choose to delete the records in the most efficient way?

Use Data Loader to mass delete the records

So deleting the one account record handles all 15 contacts in a single step. If you restore the account from the Recycle Bin, the children come back too. wrong.Use Data Loader to mass delete the recor: Data Loader is for large bulk jobs; preparing a CSV of IDs for 16 records is slower than deleting the account.
wrong.Select each contact record and delete on: Deleting contacts first isn't required; deleting the account removes them automatically.

cards.prompt: The Cosmic Computing call center manager has requested a new Case report to analyze how long individual call center staff take to accept cases. Add a row-level formula that calculates the difference between 'Date/Time Opened' and 'Case Accepted Time Stamp' in the new report.
Add a bucket column that calculates the difference between 'Date/Time Opened' and 'Case Accepted Time Stamp' in the new report.
Add the standard 'Case Age' field to the new report as this captures the difference between 'Date/Time Opened' and 'Case Accepted Time Stamp'.
answer: Add a row-level formula that calculates the difference between 'Date/Time Opened' and 'Case Accepted Time Stamp' in the new report.
cards.why: A row-level formula is a formula column you add inside a single report in Lightning Report Builder; it calculates a value for each row without creating a field on the object. Here it subtracts 'Date/Time Opened' from 'Case Accepted Time Stamp' to show acceptance time for each case. Because it lives only in the report, the Case object isn't modified. Rule of thumb: calculation per row, report only = row-level formula; calculation on group totals = summary formula.

translate.situation: Measure time-to-accept per agent, without adding a field to Case.
translate.see: A new column in the report showing hours between opened and accepted.

cards.strip: Report · difference between two date/times per case · don't change object → Row-level formula

wrong.Create a new Case custom formula field t: That works technically but modifies the Case object, which the question forbids.
wrong.Add a bucket column that calculates the: Bucket columns group values into categories (like Small/Medium/Large); they can't calculate the difference between two fields.
wrong.Add the standard 'Case Age' field to the: Case Age measures time from opened to closed (or to now), not to a custom accepted time stamp.

cards.prompt: What situations can trigger an auto-response rule?

cards.prompt: On each opportunity record, a Salesforce administrator needs to display the name of the parent account related to an account that is associated with the opportunity. How can this be accomplished?

Add a custom field with an account lookup.
Create a cross-object formula field to reference the parent account name.
Create a custom field with a dependent lookup filter on the account.
answer: Create a cross-object formula field to reference the parent account name.
cards.why: A cross-object formula field reads fields from related parent records. On Opportunity you create a formula (Text) like Account.Parent.Name, which walks Opportunity → Account → Parent Account → Name. It updates automatically whenever the parent account changes, with no automation needed. Formulas can reach up to 10 relationships away. Rule of thumb: 'display a field from a parent or grandparent' = cross-object formula.

translate.situation: Show the account's parent company on the deal.
translate.see: A read-only field on the opportunity showing the parent account name, always current.
translate.notOther: A flow copy goes stale and adds work; the formula looks it up live.

cards.strip: Opportunity · show account's parent name · read-only related value → cross-object formula

wrong.Add a custom field with an account looku: A new lookup would make users pick the parent account manually; it doesn't pull the existing parent account automatically.
wrong.Create a custom field with a dependent l: Lookup filters restrict what can be selected; they don't display a related record's value.

cards.prompt: How can support agents, who use the Case Feed, complete repetitive tasks quickly and consistently?

cards.prompt: After an Account Plan is completed it goes to a Sales Manager for approval. A Sales Manager has reviewed the plan but would like to update one of the fields in the plan before approving it. What is true regarding editing records that have been submitted for approval?

In the approval process you can also allow 'Administrators OR the currently assigned approver' to edit, so the Sales Manager can update the field before approving. cards.prompt: An events company uses a screen flow in an Experience cloud site to capture event cancellation requests. cards.prompt: Cosmic Telecom wants to understand what protects the org from a customer trying to manipulate the agent into ignoring its instructions or revealing internal system prompts. Which Salesforce feature is primarily responsible for this kind of protection?

cards.prompt: Cosmic Solutions wants a basic understanding of what Agentforce actually does before rolling it out. Which statement best describes Agentforce's core capability compared to a traditional Salesforce automation tool like Flow?

Agentforce is a rules engine that only follows exact if/then branching logic defined in advance, identical to flow
answer: Agentforce can autonomously reason over a request, select the appropriate action, and execute it without a human predefining every branch of logic
cards.why: Agentforce agents use an LLM-powered reasoning engine (the Atlas Reasoning Engine) to understand a request, pick the right topic and action, run it, and respond. You give it topics, instructions, and actions, but you don't map out every possible branch like in Flow. Flow, by contrast, runs only the exact steps and decisions an admin built. Rule of thumb: Flow = predefined path; Agentforce = reasons to choose the path.
cards.strip: Agentforce vs. Flow · core capability · autonomy → reasons, picks action, executes without predefined branches

wrong.Agentforce can only generate text respon: Agents can run actions, like flows, Apex, and record updates, not just generate text.
wrong.Agentforce requires a developer to write: Many actions are standard or built with flows and prompt templates; no Apex is needed for every request.
wrong.Agentforce is a rules engine that only f: That describes Flow. Agentforce's difference is that it reasons instead of following preset branches.

cards.prompt: A Salesforce Administrator needs to insert custom object records on a weekly basis. The number of records that need to be inserted often exceeds 60,000. There may also be the possibility of duplicate records, which the organization does not want. What is the best way for the Salesforce Administrator to load the records?
options: Run a Batch Import class
Use the Data Import Wizard
Use a third-party data import tool
Use Duplicate Management and import the records via Data Loader
answer: Use Duplicate Management and import the records via Data Loader
cards.why: Data Loader is a desktop app for bulk data work that handles up to 5 million records, so 60,000+ is fine. Data Import Wizard tops out at 50,000 records per import. Duplicate management (matching rules plus duplicate rules) applies to records created through the API, so Data Loader inserts that match an existing record can be blocked. Rule of thumb: over 50,000 records = Data Loader; prevent duplicates = duplicate rules.
cards.traps: Import Wizard's built-in duplicate checking tempts you, but the 50,000-record limit rules it out.
cards.strip: Weekly load · 60,000+ records + no duplicates · volume over 50k → Duplicate Management + Data Loader

wrong.Run a Batch Import class: Writing Apex batch code isn't necessary when Data Loader handles this declaratively.
wrong.Use the Data Import Wizard: Data Import Wizard is limited to 50,000 records per import, below the 60,000+ needed.
wrong.Use a third-party data import tool: A paid third-party tool isn't needed; Salesforce's own Data Loader handles the volume.

cards.prompt: GN International Inc. uses Salesforce for managing their sales activities and they have created various custom objects. The Sales manager requested the Administrator to create a new report with certain information. When attempting to define the custom report type, the Administrator discovered that certain fields could not be added. Which of the following field types can NOT be added to a custom report?
options: Product fields
History fields
Product schedule fields
Account Fields
answer: History fields
Product schedule fields
cards.why: When defining a custom report type you choose which fields are available. Salesforce doesn't allow some fields in custom report types: history fields (field change history), product schedule fields, and the Age field on cases and opportunities. Use the standard history report types instead. Rule of thumb: custom report types exclude history, product schedule, and Age fields.
cards.strip: Custom report type · fields that can't be added · exclusions → History fields, Product schedule fields

wrong.Product fields: Product fields can be added to custom report types that include products.
wrong.Account Fields: Account fields can be added to custom report types, directly or via lookup.

cards.prompt: The ownership of a case needs to be transferred from one customer support user to another. The role hierarchy is set up with a customer support role and a support manager role above. Who can change the ownership of the case?
options: The support manager
The current owner of the case
Any user with the customer support role
All users
The Salesforce Administrator
answer: The support manager
The current owner of the case
The Salesforce Administrator
cards.why: Changing a record's owner needs edit-level rights plus being in the right position. The current owner can transfer their own case. Users above the owner in the role hierarchy (the support manager) can transfer it because hierarchy gives them owner-like access. The administrator can transfer any record via Modify All Data or Transfer Record permissions. Rule of thumb: owner, people above the owner, and admins.
cards.traps: Same-role peers seem like they'd have access, but hierarchy only goes upward.
cards.strip: Case ownership change · who can · hierarchy and permissions → support manager, current owner, admin

wrong.Any user with the customer support role: Peers in the same role don't automatically get rights to each other's cases.
wrong.All users: Most users don't have permission to transfer other people's records.

cards.prompt: Sam has created a matching rule on the Contact object to detect duplicates. What is true in this situation?
options: Only one field can be used for matching in the matching rule
Duplicate contacts will be blocked or allowed based on the setting in the Duplicate Rule
Only one duplicate rule can be active at one time
Nothing will happen unless a duplicate rule is defined that uses the matching rule
answer: Duplicate contacts will be blocked or allowed based on the setting in the Duplicate Rule
Nothing will happen unless a duplicate rule is defined that uses the matching rule
cards.why: Duplicate management has two parts: a matching rule defines how to compare records (which fields, exact or fuzzy), and a duplicate rule says what to do when the matching rule finds a match (block or allow with a warning, and whether to report). A matching rule by itself does nothing; a duplicate rule must reference it. Rule of thumb: matching rule = how to compare; duplicate rule = what to do.

translate.situation: Stop duplicate contacts.
translate.feature: Matching rule (what counts as a duplicate) + Duplicate rule (what to do about it).
translate.see: A warning or a block when saving a look-alike contact.
translate.notOther: A matching rule alone does nothing; multiple fields and multiple active duplicate rules are allowed.

cards.traps: Thinking the matching rule alone blocks duplicates.
cards.strip: Matching rule on Contact · what's true · two-part setup → duplicate rule decides block/allow; nothing without it

wrong.Only one field can be used for matching: A matching rule can compare up to 10 fields.
wrong.Only one duplicate rule can be active at: Up to 5 active duplicate rules are allowed per object.

cards.prompt: Super Computers Inc. stores purchase information in a custom object. The purchase manager wants to analyze the trend of purchases for which she needs historical data. The Salesforce Administrator decided to create a reporting snapshot. The Salesforce Administrator is considering which reports can be used as the source to build a snapshot. Which report formats can be used to create a reporting snapshot?
options: Summary Report
Tabular Report
Joined Report
Matrix Report
answer: Summary Report
Tabular Report
cards.why: A reporting snapshot copies the results of a source report into a custom object on a schedule, building up historical data for trend reporting. The source report must be tabular or summary. Matrix and joined reports aren't supported as sources. Rule of thumb: snapshot source = tabular or summary.
cards.strip: Reporting snapshot · source report formats · allowed → Tabular, Summary

wrong.Joined Report: Joined reports can't be used as a reporting snapshot source.
wrong.Matrix Report: Matrix reports can't be used as a reporting snapshot source.

cards.prompt: A data file containing contact records is automatically sent to a computer every day. The Salesforce Administrator needs to automatically load contact records from this file into Salesforce at 6 PM daily. Which tools are best suited for the requirement?
options: Run a batch class to insert the records
Data Loader via user interface
Use an AppExchange tool such as Jitterbit Data Loader
Data Loader via command-line interface
answer: Use an AppExchange tool such as Jitterbit Data Loader
Data Loader via command-line interface
cards.why: The requirement is an unattended daily load at a fixed time. Data Loader's command-line interface (Windows) can be scheduled with an operating system scheduler like Windows Task Scheduler. Third-party tools from AppExchange, like Jitterbit Data Loader, have built-in scheduling. Rule of thumb: scheduled automatic loads = Data Loader CLI or a third-party scheduler.

translate.situation: Load a file into Salesforce every day at 6 PM with nobody clicking.
translate.feature: Data Loader command line, or Jitterbit.
translate.see: A scheduled job that imports automatically.
translate.notOther: The Data Loader UI needs someone to run it; a batch class is code.

cards.traps: Data Loader UI looks right, but it can't be scheduled.
cards.strip: Daily file · automatic load at 6 PM · scheduled → Data Loader CLI or Jitterbit

wrong.Run a batch class to insert the records: Apex can't read a file sitting on a local computer, and it's code rather than a data tool.
wrong.Data Loader via user interface: The Data Loader screen needs a person to click through each import; it can't run at 6 PM by itself.

cards.prompt: An organization has multi-currency enabled. What can cause a record in an import file to fail?
options: The record fails system validation rules
Currency in the file is an inactive Salesforce currency
The record fails custom validation rules
Currency field is left blank
answer: The record fails system validation rules
The record fails custom validation rules
cards.why: Any import, single or multi-currency, fails for a row if it breaks rules on save: system validation (like a required field being blank or a value in the wrong format) or custom validation rules. Currency problems are handled differently: if the Currency ISO Code is blank, Salesforce uses the importing user's personal currency. Rule of thumb: validation failures stop rows; currency issues are defaulted.

translate.situation: Know why an imported row gets rejected.
translate.see: Rows missing required fields or breaking validation rules fail.
translate.notOther: Blank or inactive currencies don't fail; the user's currency is used.

cards.strip: Multi-currency import · what fails a record · save-time rules → system validation + custom validation rules

wrong.Currency in the file is an inactive Sale: Per this deck's key, an inactive currency code doesn't fail the record; the importer's personal currency is used instead.
wrong.Currency field is left blank: A blank currency doesn't fail the import; the record gets the importing user's personal currency.

cards.prompt: Quotes that are discounted more than 20% need approval from the Sales Director. How can this requirement be met?
options: Create a record-triggered flow to assign the quote to the Sales Director
Create an approval process on the quote with an entry criteria on the quote discount percentage
Create an approval process on the opportunity with an entry criteria on the opportunity discount percentage
Create a validation rule to check the discount percentage
answer: Create an approval process on the quote with an entry criteria on the quote discount percentage
cards.why: An approval process routes a record to approvers and locks it until a decision. Create it on the Quote object (Setup > Approval Processes) with entry criteria 'Discount > 20%' and the Sales Director as approver. Quotes over 20% then require approval when submitted. Rule of thumb: 'needs approval from someone' = approval process on the object holding the data.

translate.situation: Big discounts on quotes need the director's sign-off.
translate.feature: Approval process on the Quote object.
translate.see: Quotes over 20% off get routed to the director.
translate.notOther: The discount lives on the Quote, so the approval goes there, not on Opportunity.

cards.traps: Right tool on the wrong object (opportunity vs. quote).
cards.strip: Quote discount > 20% · needs Director approval · approve/reject → approval process on Quote

wrong.Create a record-triggered flow to assign: Changing ownership isn't an approval; there's no approve/reject or record lock.
wrong.Create an approval process on the opport: The discount lives on the quote, and an opportunity can have several quotes; approval belongs on the Quote.
wrong.Create a validation rule to check the di: A validation rule would just block saving; it can't route anything for approval.

cards.prompt: An admin has been notified that some users can no longer execute screen flows from record pages. What should an admin do as part of troubleshooting permission-related issues?
options: Reactivate the FlowSites permission.
Assign the Run Flows permission to users via a permission set or profile.
Enable the Flow User checkbox on the user detail page in Setup.
Grant the Manage Flow permission to all users.
answer: Assign the Run Flows permission to users via a permission set or profile.
cards.why: To run a screen flow, users need flow access: the 'Run Flows' user permission on a profile or permission set (or access granted to the specific flow). If users suddenly can't run flows, check whether that permission was removed or a profile change dropped it, then assign it via a permission set. Rule of thumb: 'users can't run a flow' = check Run Flows.

translate.situation: Users suddenly can't run a screen flow.
translate.see: The flow button works again for those users.
translate.notOther: Flow User / Manage Flow give far more than needed; FlowSites is deprecated.

cards.traps: Manage Flow (build) vs. Run Flows (use).
cards.strip: Screen flows · users can't run · permission → Run Flows via profile/permission set

FlowSites relates to running flows for site guest users, not internal users on record pages.
wrong.Enable the Flow User checkbox on the use: The Flow User checkbox is a legacy feature-license approach; the standard fix is granting Run Flows through a profile or permission set.
wrong.Grant the Manage Flow permission to all: Manage Flow lets users create and edit flows, which is far too much access just to run one.

cards.prompt: The finance department at Universal Rentals would like the Salesforce Administrator to implement manager approvals for Paid Time Off requests. What is true regarding the approval process capabilities?
options: Approval requests can be sent via Chatter for any standard or custom object that has been enabled for feed tracking
Records are always locked for all users during an approval process
If enabled, an approver can receive and reply to approval requests via email
Approval requests can only be assigned to users
answer: Approval requests can be sent via Chatter for any standard or custom object that has been enabled for feed tracking
If enabled, an approver can receive and reply to approval requests via email
cards.why: Approval processes have flexible notification options. If Approvals in Chatter is enabled, approval requests appear as Chatter posts for objects with feed tracking, and approvers can approve from there. With email approval response enabled, approvers can reply 'Approve' or 'Reject' directly to the email. Rule of thumb: approvals can be answered in Chatter or by email reply.
cards.traps: 'Always' and 'only' wording.
cards.strip: Approval process · true capabilities · notification options → Chatter approvals; email reply approvals

wrong.Records are always locked for all users: Admins can always edit locked records, and the process can let the current approver edit too, so it's not 'all users.'
wrong.Approval requests can only be assigned t: Approvers can also be queues or a related user field like Manager.

cards.prompt: Cosmic Global wants to ensure that no opportunities are lost if a sales rep forgets to follow up. At least 200 records are being created a day. A reminder task should be created automatically 15 days after the 'Created Date' of the opportunity. Which automation feature can be used to address the requirement declaratively considering the risk of exceeding governor limits per transaction?
options: Flow Builder
Big Deal Alert
Apex Trigger
Approval Process
answer: Flow Builder
cards.why: A record-triggered flow on Opportunity can use a scheduled path set to 15 days after Created Date to create the reminder task. Scheduled paths run in batches separately from the original save, so 200+ records a day don't hit per-transaction governor limits (Salesforce's resource caps per transaction). It's built in Flow Builder with no code. Rule of thumb: 'do something X days after a date' = record-triggered flow with a scheduled path.

translate.situation: Create a follow-up task 15 days after each new deal.
translate.feature: Record-triggered flow with a Scheduled Path.
translate.see: A task appears automatically on day 15.
translate.notOther: Apex isn't needed; Big Deal Alert only emails; approvals are sign-offs.

cards.strip: Opportunity · task 15 days after creation, 200+/day · declarative + limits → Flow Builder (scheduled path)

wrong.Big Deal Alert: Big Deal Alerts email people when a large opportunity hits a probability and amount threshold; they can't create tasks later.
wrong.Apex Trigger: Apex is code, and the question asks for a declarative (no-code) solution.
wrong.Approval Process: Approval processes route records for approval; they don't schedule reminder tasks.

cards.prompt: A sales rep asked an Admin to look for soft-deleted Invoice records. How long does a deleted record stay in the Recycle Bin?
options: 30 days
15 days
Until the Recycle Bin is emptied using the user interface
Until the Recycle Bin reaches a certain size
Forever
answer: 15 days
Until the Recycle Bin is emptied using the user interface
Until the Recycle Bin reaches a certain size
cards.why: Deleted records go to the Recycle Bin, where they stay for 15 days before permanent deletion. They're removed sooner if someone empties the Recycle Bin. The bin also has a size limit (25 times your org's MB of storage, in records); when it's full, the oldest records are automatically purged. Rule of thumb: 15 days, or sooner if emptied or full.
cards.traps: 30 days is the classic wrong number.
cards.strip: Recycle Bin · how long records stay · retention rules → 15 days, until emptied, or until size limit

wrong.30 days: The Recycle Bin keeps deleted records for 15 days, not 30.
wrong.Forever: Records don't stay forever; they're permanently deleted after 15 days or sooner.

cards.prompt: A Salesforce Admin is building a screen flow to power a dynamic partner onboarding experience. The admin is using a Data Graph to retrieve consolidated partner data from multiple objects and sources. The next step is to transform that unified data into a format that can be easily displayed on a screen component and later updated in Salesforce. Which Flow feature supports this requirement?
options: Use an External Services registration to convert Data Graph values into JSON
Use a Custom Metadata Type to map the data graph to a screen component
Use a Data Transform element to reshape the Data Graph output in Flow Builder
Use the Assignment element to split the Data Graph fields into individual variables
answer: Use a Data Transform element to reshape the Data Graph output in Flow Builder
cards.why: A Data Graph (in Data Cloud) bundles related data from multiple objects and sources into one structure. Flow Builder's Transform element (Data Transform) maps and reshapes data from one structure to another, like turning Data Graph output into the record or collection shape a screen component expects. It's visual, without code. Rule of thumb: reshape data inside a flow = Transform element.
cards.strip: Flow · reshape Data Graph output for screen · mapping → Transform element

wrong.Use an External Services registration to: External Services connects flows to outside APIs; it isn't a data reshaping tool.
wrong.Use a Custom Metadata Type to map the da: Custom metadata stores configuration values; it doesn't transform runtime data.
wrong.Use the Assignment element to split the: Assignment sets values one by one; it's clumsy and doesn't map complex structures like Transform does.

cards.prompt: The Sales manager of Cosmic Solutions has been assigned a task to create an automated system for processing discounts on Opportunities. Discount rates of up to 40% require the Sales Manager's approval. If the discount rate is more than 40%, it requires the CEO's approval. Which Salesforce automation solution is appropriate for this scenario?
options: Schema Builder
Flow Builder
Apex Trigger
Approval Process
answer: Approval Process
cards.why: An approval process supports multiple approval steps with criteria. Step 1 sends discounts up to 40% to the Sales Manager. Step 2 (or a separate entry path) sends discounts over 40% to the CEO. Records lock during approval and approvers can approve or reject. Rule of thumb: tiered approvals = approval process with multiple steps.
cards.traps: Flow is the default automation answer, but formal approvals still point to Approval Process.
cards.strip: Opportunity discounts · tiered approvals (Manager/CEO) · approve/reject → Approval Process

wrong.Schema Builder: Schema Builder is a visual data model tool for viewing and creating objects and fields; it doesn't automate anything.
wrong.Flow Builder: Flow can automate many things, but the question is about routing for human approval, which is an approval process's job.
wrong.Apex Trigger: Apex is code and doesn't give built-in approval routing.

cards.prompt: Cosmic Solutions has a custom object called Weekly Employee Summary, which stores a summary of employee data that is tracked in Salesforce, such as hours worked and wage totals. An autolaunched flow has been built to calculate this information and create a new Weekly Employee Summary record for each employee every time it is run. Currently, a Salesforce Administrator needs to run this flow manually once a week. They would like this type of operation to be run automatically in the future. Which solutions would meet this requirement?
options: Invoke the flow from an Apex job that runs weekly.
Use a TimeSync Automation Rule to run the flow weekly.
Invoke the flow from a schedule-triggered flow.
Configure the flow on the 'Scheduled Jobs' page in Setup.
answer: Invoke the flow from an Apex job that runs weekly.
Invoke the flow from a schedule-triggered flow.
cards.why: To run something weekly without a person, you need a scheduler. A schedule-triggered flow can run weekly and call the existing autolaunched flow as a subflow. A developer could also write a scheduled Apex job that runs weekly and starts the flow. Rule of thumb: run on a timer = schedule-triggered flow (no code) or scheduled Apex (code).
cards.traps: Made-up feature names and the read-only Scheduled Jobs page.
cards.strip: Autolaunched flow · run weekly automatically · scheduler → schedule-triggered flow or weekly Apex job

wrong.Use a TimeSync Automation Rule to run th: There's no 'TimeSync Automation Rule' feature in Salesforce.
wrong.Configure the flow on the 'Scheduled Job: The Scheduled Jobs page shows and deletes jobs already scheduled; you can't set up a flow schedule there.

cards.prompt: CosmicTech Solutions is implementing custom agent actions to enhance its customer service processes. The development team needs to ensure that each action is correctly configured and functions as expected. Which core component of a custom agent action should the development team review during configuration?
options: Action Instructions
Context Variables
Classification Descriptions
Language Settings
answer: Action Instructions
cards.why: A custom agent action has instructions that tell the agent what the action does and when to use it, plus input and output instructions that describe each parameter. The reasoning engine reads these to decide whether to pick the action and how to fill its inputs. Poor instructions are the most common reason an action isn't chosen or gets bad inputs. Rule of thumb: agent picks actions based on their instructions.
cards.traps: Classification description belongs to topics, not actions.
cards.strip: Custom agent action · what to review · how agent decides to use it → Action Instructions

wrong.Context Variables: Context variables pass session data (like the user's record ID) into the conversation; they're not the core of an action's definition.
wrong.Classification Descriptions: Topics have classification descriptions that help the agent pick a topic; that's topic-level, not action-level.
wrong.Language Settings: Language settings control the agent's supported languages, not how an action is configured.

cards.prompt: What is true regarding the addition of a report chart to the Service Console in Classic?
options: The source report of the chart must be a Summary or Matrix report
The source report must contain a chart
The report must be added to the service console page layout
The report chart must be added to the page layout of the object from which to display the chart
The source report of the chart must always be a Joined report
answer: The source report of the chart must be a Summary or Matrix report
The source report must contain a chart
The report chart must be added to the page layout of the object from which to display the chart
cards.why: In the Salesforce Classic Service Console, you can show a report chart on a record page. The source report must be summary or matrix (charts need groupings) and must already have a chart. Then you add the report chart to the page layout of the object where it should appear, and set filters so it shows data related to that record. Rule of thumb: chart needs grouped report + chart + placed on the object's layout.

translate.situation: Show a chart in the console sidebar while agents work.
translate.feature: Report chart as a console component.
translate.see: A chart beside the record, from a grouped report that already has a chart.
translate.notOther: Joined reports aren't supported; the chart goes on the object's layout, not a 'console layout'.

cards.strip: Classic console report chart · requirements · embedded chart → summary/matrix + has chart + on object's layout

wrong.The report must be added to the service: There isn't a separate 'service console page layout'; the chart goes on the object's page layout.
wrong.The source report of the chart must alwa: Joined reports aren't supported for embedded report charts; summary or matrix are required.

cards.prompt: The support supervisors of a call center that uses Service Cloud Omni-Channel would like to see which of their support reps have been accepting cases recently and whether they are online, offline, or busy. They should be able to filter reps by status and see reps with a particular status only each time they log in. Which of the following is the best place to do so in the Omni-Channel Supervisor?
options: Service Reps Tab
Work Tab
In Progress Work Tab
Users Tab
answer: Service Reps Tab
cards.why: Omni-Channel Supervisor is the supervisor's dashboard for routing. The Service Reps tab (formerly Agents tab) lists each rep with their presence status (online, busy, away, offline), current work, and recent accepted work. Supervisors can filter by status, and those filters are saved so the same view loads next time. Rule of thumb: watch reps and status = Service Reps tab.

translate.situation: Supervisors watch who's online and taking work.
translate.see: Each rep's status, current work, capacity, last accept time; filters stick.
translate.notOther: In Progress Work is by queue; 'Work' and 'Users' tabs don't exist.

cards.strip: Omni-Channel Supervisor · reps' status + recent work, saved filters → Service Reps tab

wrong.Work Tab: The Work tab shows routed work items waiting or assigned, not reps' status.
wrong.In Progress Work Tab: This shows work currently being handled, focused on items rather than reps' presence.
wrong.Users Tab: There's no Users tab in Omni-Channel Supervisor.

cards.prompt: Which of the following are true about configuring Web-to-Case?
options: A default response template may be selected
A maximum number of cases that can be created daily must be set
HTML code must be generated and can be added to multiple websites
A default case owner must be selected
Only Standard case object fields can be captured on the webform
answer: A default response template may be selected
HTML code must be generated and can be added to multiple websites
A default case owner must be selected
cards.why: Web-to-Case turns website form submissions into cases. In Setup you enable it, choose a default case origin, and optionally a default response template for auto-replies. A default case owner must be set in Support Settings so cases have an owner when no assignment rule matches. You then generate HTML that can be pasted into any number of websites. Rule of thumb: Web-to-Case = enable, default owner, generate HTML, optional response template.
cards.traps: The daily limit exists but isn't admin-configurable.
cards.strip: Web-to-Case · setup truths · configuration → optional template, reusable HTML, default owner

wrong.A maximum number of cases that can be cr: Salesforce fixes the limit at 5,000 cases per day; admins don't set it.
wrong.Only Standard case object fields can be: Custom case fields can be included when generating the form.
